entities.label: Person
entities.summary: Julius Pollux was a Greek scholar and rhetorician from Naucratis, Roman Egypt, who held the professor-chair of rhetoric in Athens at the Academy, as appointed by Emperor Commodus. This appointment was due to his exceptional melodious voice, according to Philostratus' Lives of the Sophists. Pollux was a prominent figure in the cultural and intellectual landscape of the Roman Empire, and his work had a lasting impact on the development of rhetoric and education. His legacy extends beyond his own time, as his writings and teachings influenced later scholars and thinkers. Pollux's appointment by Commodus not only highlighted his exceptional talent but also underscored the emperor's patronage of the arts and learning. Despite the passing of centuries, Pollux's contributions to the field of rhetoric remain relevant today, making him an important figure in the annals of intellectual history.
